Find which term each string contains, in parallel

Source: R/par-match-term.R
par_match_term.Rd

For each string in x:

  • par_match_term() finds the index of the first term in terms it contains. It is like match() for substrings.

  • par_count_term() counts every hit of every term, such as to score strings against a lexicon of positive and negative words. With weights, it sums a score per hit instead.

  • par_which_term() finds every term the string contains, such as every drug an abstract names.

  • par_match_term_all() returns every pair of a string and a term it contains, with the number of hits. This is a document-term matrix in long form.

  • par_locate_term_all() finds where each hit is, such as to highlight terms or show them in context.

Usage

par_match_term(
  x,
  terms,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  whole_word = FALSE,
  fixed = TRUE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

par_count_term(
  x,
  terms,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  whole_word = FALSE,
  fixed = TRUE,
  weights = NULL,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

par_which_term(
  x,
  terms,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  whole_word = FALSE,
  fixed = TRUE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

par_match_term_all(
  x,
  terms,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  whole_word = FALSE,
  fixed = TRUE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

par_locate_term_all(
  x,
  terms,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  whole_word = FALSE,
  fixed = TRUE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

Arguments

x

A string vector, or an object convertible by as.character().

terms

A string vector of literal strings to find. NA is not allowed.

ignore_case

If TRUE, letters match regardless of case, in any script: "é" matches "É". ASCII letters cost nothing extra. Strings with other characters are lowercased first. With fixed = FALSE, this is (?i).

whole_word

If TRUE, a term counts only where it isn't part of a longer word. "york" then matches "new york" and "york, uk", but not "yorkshire". The characters right before and after the term must not be word characters, those \\w matches. These are letters, digits, and marks (such as an accent written as a character of its own) in any script, and _. An apostrophe (' or the curly \u2019) between two word characters joins them into one word. So "won" doesn't match "won't", nor "heaven" "heaven's". With fixed = FALSE, the same goes for a term's match.

If "start", a term must start a word but may end inside one, as a prefix: "happ" matches "happy" and "happiness", but not "unhappy". This is the "happ*" of dictionaries such as LIWC.

fixed

If FALSE, terms are regexes, in the syntax of par_detect().

nthreads

A whole number: the max number of threads to use. 0 means the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable, or else all cores. The default is the parvenu.threads option, or 0 if that isn't set. Inputs too small to keep that many threads busy get fewer, and more threads than cores count as all cores.

weights

For par_count_term(): NULL to count hits, or a numeric vector as long as terms, without NA. Each hit then adds the weight of its term, as for a lexicon that rates words from -5 to 5.

Value

  • par_match_term(): an integer vector as long as x, with the position in terms of the first term found in each string. NA if none is found, or where x is NA. Use terms[par_match_term(x, terms)] to get the terms themselves.

  • par_count_term(): an integer vector as long as x, with the number of hits in each string, or NA where x is NA. Every occurrence of every term counts, also where they overlap. So "new york" has two hits for c("new york", "york"), and a term listed twice counts twice. For regexes, each term's matches are counted as par_count() counts them, which don't overlap. With weights, it returns a double vector: the sum of the weights of the hits, 0 if none.

  • par_which_term(): a list as long as x. Each element has the positions in terms of every term found in the string, in increasing order and each once. It is integer(0) if none, or NA where x is NA.

  • par_match_term_all(): a data frame with one row per pair, sorted by x and then by term. Column x is a position in x, term is a position in terms found there, and n is the number of its hits, as par_count_term() counts them. Strings with no term, and NA, have no rows.

  • par_locate_term_all(): a data frame with one row per hit, the hits that par_count_term() counts, sorted by x, then by start, then by term. Columns x and term are as above. start and end are the positions of the first and last characters of the hit, as in par_locate(). An empty term's hit has end one less than start. Strings with no term, and NA, have no rows.

Details

Terms are literal, as in grepl(fixed = TRUE), so no character needs escaping. With fixed = FALSE, they are regular expressions.

Order sets priority. If a string contains several terms, the one earliest in terms wins, wherever it occurs in the string. Put specific terms before general ones, such as "new york" before "york".

All terms are compiled into one Aho-Corasick automaton. It finds every occurrence of every term in a single pass over each string, however many terms there are. The last automaton is kept, so calls that repeat the same terms don't build it again. The threads read the strings straight from R's memory, as data.table does.

With fixed = FALSE, the terms are compiled into one regex set instead. It also finds in one pass which terms match a string. That is much slower than the automaton, but much faster than a regex per term.

Examples

cities <- c("new york", "york", "paris")

par_match_term(c("york and new york", "paris, texas", "rome", NA), cities)
#> [1]  1  3 NA NA

par_match_term("NEW YORK", cities, ignore_case = TRUE)
#> [1] 1

par_match_term(c("yorkshire", "york, uk"), cities, whole_word = TRUE)
#> [1] NA  2

par_match_term("1+1=2", c("+", "("))
#> [1] 1

par_count_term("good food, not bad", c("good", "bad"), whole_word = TRUE)
#> [1] 2

par_count_term("happy, unhappy, happiness", "happ", whole_word = "start")
#> [1] 2

par_count_term("good food, not bad", c("good", "bad"), weights = c(1, -2))
#> [1] -1

par_which_term(c("york and new york", "rome", NA), cities)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> integer(0)
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] NA
#> 

par_match_term_all(c("york and new york", "rome", NA), cities)
#>   x term n
#> 1 1    1 1
#> 2 1    2 2

par_locate_term_all(c("york and new york", "rome", NA), cities)
#>   x term start end
#> 1 1    2     1   4
#> 2 1    1    10  17
#> 3 1    2    14  17

par_match_term(c("call 555-1234", "mail a@b.org"), c("\\d{3}-\\d{4}", "@"), fixed = FALSE)
#> [1] 1 2
